chapter_title: Concerning the Catechumen who found fault with the Elect: why he is angry.
chapter_note: This chapter is largely a pastoral/homiletic rebuke framed as dialogue, applying Manichaean cosmological anthropology to community discipline (catechumen vs. elect). Only brief doctrinal fragments (divine element from the heights; alien body/flesh of Sin; two essences) plausibly preserve older teaching, but they are embedded in institutional address and may already be Mani-era church redaction rather than the oldest substrate.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic narrative setup (“Once again… my master, the apostle”) and dialogue staging mark hagiographic/editorial frame.
Dialogue content serving as the catechumen’s complaint; functions as narrative scaffold rather than impersonal cosmological exposition.
Speech-attribution formula (“Then our enlightener speaks…”) is a classic compilation frame marker.

Direct admonition plus an illustrative analogy (tree/smoke) aimed at correcting behavior; application voice (“know and understand… rather…”) and moral-pastoral purpose dominate, not cosmos→cosmos mapping.

paragraphs.core_text: “They are gods as they stand firm in the image of the gods. The divinity that is planted in them came to them from the heights and [dw]elt in them.”
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed institutional anchoring and moral conclusion: opening applicative clause (“This is also the case with the elect.”) and closing performance claim (“They have done the will of the greatness.”). Kept the anthropological/cosmological statement about indwelling divinity from the heights.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Embedded doctrinal anthropology (divinity ‘from the heights’ dwelling within) suggests older cosmological teaching, but it is grafted into a community category (‘elect’) in the surrounding sentence, indicating later pastoral deployment.

paragraphs.core_text: “You know, once and for all, they are established in a body that is not their own, hating the flesh of Sin that makes the other dwell in a foreign land.”
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed behavior/exhortation material: the lead-in about elect cursing each other, the reassurance (“do not you be troubled in your heart”), and the application/consequence about anger and ‘hard words’. Kept the causal cosmological anthropology about alien embodiment and the agency of Sin.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Causal mechanics of alien embodiment (“body that is not their own… foreign land”) is characteristic of Manichaean cosmology; the paragraph’s opening and closing are pastoral application to intra-community conflict.

paragraphs.core_text: “For you have known the mystery of the two essences, you have understood that what is good and what is evil dwell in every person.”
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed repeated imperatives and community-discipline prohibitions (“do not… criticise… speak against… reject…”), plus institutional language about ‘saints’ and ‘burden’ used to enforce deference. Kept the compact doctrinal claim (two essences; good/evil co-dwelling).
paragraphs.temporal_note: The ‘two essences’ doctrine is a core cosmological axiom, but here it is pressed into pastoral regulation of speech/attitude toward the elect; the paragraph is dominantly application voice.
Second-person moral accusation and community-teacher rhetoric (sins, conduct, being taught) are pastoral/institutional, even though ‘Cross of Light’ is cosmological vocabulary.
Pure exhortation toward honoring the elect; direct application voice throughout.
Narrative transition and reaction report (“Then, when the apostle had uttered…”)—hagiographic framing/closure mechanics.

Penitential address (“Forgive me my sins”) and moralizing explanation. Phrase “the old man” may echo later Christian/Pauline idiom, but it appears here within a catechetical/pastoral context rather than impersonal cosmological exposition.
